documents.title: Tahoe Itinerary
documents.body:
Tahoe Itinerary

Tahoe Crew: Grace, Sam, Theo, and Mia

Cabin: 88 Snowberry Hollow Rd, Tahoe City, CA 96145. Check-in after 3 PM, check-out by 10 AM. The lockbox code is pinned in the group chat.

Day 1: Arrive
- Mia + Theo: flight LAX → RNO, departs 7:50 AM, lands 9:20 AM. Confirmation QX7M2P.
- Grace + Sam: driving up the day before with all the gear, staying over in Reno, picking us up at arrivals around 9:45.
- Grocery run in Truckee on the way in (list below).
- Afternoon: settle in, hot tub, early dinner. Grace is making her chili.

Day 2: Snowshoe
- 9:30 AM at Tahoe Meadows. Rentals are reserved under Grace.
- Packed lunch on the trail, thermos of hot chocolate.
- Dinner: Theo's on tacos.

Day 3: Lake day
- Slow morning, coffee on the deck.
- Afternoon drive along the west shore.
- 3:30 PM sunset shoot at Emerald Bay, Inspiration Point lot.
- Dinner: Mia's olive focaccia and a big pot of minestrone. Gift swap after dinner (under $30).

Day 4: Head home
- Pack up and tidy by 9:30, out the door by 10.
- Two cars down 395: Mia rides with Sam, Theo rides with Grace. Lunch stop in Bishop.
- Home in time for dinner.

Shared costs
- Cabin: $840 total, $210 each. Venmo Grace.
- Groceries: split four ways. Sam is keeping the receipts.
- Gas: drivers cover it, riders buy lunch.

Group grocery list
- Coffee, oat milk, eggs, tortillas
- Chili and taco fixings
- Bread flour, olives, rosemary (Mia)
- Trail snacks and clementines
- Hot chocolate and marshmallows

Good to know
- Check road conditions and chain controls before every drive.
- Bear box for all trash. Lock it every time.
- Nearest urgent care is about 10 minutes away in Tahoe City.

documents.title: Photography Workflow Guide
documents.body:
Northlight Studio: Photography Workflow Guide

Welcome to the team! This is how we take a shoot from memory card to client gallery. It's written for new assistants and freelancers, so it goes step by step. If something here doesn't match what you see on set, tell Mia or Pedro and we'll update it.

1. Before the shoot
- Format every card in camera the night before, never on a computer.
- Charge all batteries, including the strobes and the client preview tablet.
- Put the client's shot list in the shared project folder.
- Shoot a gray card frame at the start of every lighting setup.

2. Import
- Copy, don't move. Import from the card to the working SSD and the studio RAID at the same time.
- Folder name: YYMMDD_Client_Project, for example the shoot date followed by Feld_GlazeCollection.
- Apply the Northlight copyright preset and the client keywords during import.
- A card isn't safe to reuse until its files exist on two drives. Mark it with blue tape once it's backed up.

3. Culling
- The first pass is fast: flag possible picks only, no zooming. Trust your gut.
- On the second pass, compare similar frames side by side and check focus at 100%.
- Star ratings: 3 stars for the client gallery, 4 stars for retouching, 5 stars for portfolio candidates.
- Aim for about 10 percent of what was shot. Clients want good choices, not everything.

4. Color
- Start from the shoot's custom camera profile and set white balance from the gray card frame.
- Sync settings across each lighting setup, then fine-tune the hero images one by one.
- Get product colors and skin tones right before you think about mood.
- Soft-proof on the calibrated display. Never judge color on a laptop in a bright room.

5. Retouching
- Always clean up dust, stray threads, and fingerprints on products.
- Never change the shape or color of a product. What the client sells is what we show.
- Save retouched files as layered TIFFs next to the RAWs.

6. Delivery
- Export full-resolution JPEGs in sRGB, plus web crops at 1:1 and 4:5.
- File names: Client_Project_001, Client_Project_002, and so on.
- Upload to the client gallery, make sure every image loads, then send the link with a short personal note.
- Pedro sends the invoice the same day.

7. Archive
- Within a week, archive the RAWs, TIFFs, and catalog to the RAID and the cloud backup.
- Log the project and drive name in the studio archive sheet.

Questions? Mia handles color and culling. Pedro handles clients, schedules, and invoices.

documents.title: Portfolio Statement
documents.body:
Portfolio Statement: Mia Navarro

I photograph the moments right before and right after something happens: the market before the crowds arrive, the table after dinner, the ridge while the light is still deciding what color it wants to be.

I grew up in Los Angeles in a big, loud family where every Sunday dinner ended with someone pulling out a camera. I've been chasing that feeling of warmth ever since.

My travel work spans Sicily, Mexico City, the Marin Headlands, and the Nevada desert. I'm drawn to texture and ordinary light: laundry lines strung over an alley in Ortigia, red sandstone at blue hour in the Valley of Fire, steam rising off a cup of coffee in Roma Norte. I want to make pictures you feel like you could step into.

My commercial work with Northlight Studio and independent makers like Feld Ceramics comes from the same place. A handmade bowl deserves the same patience as a landscape. I light simply, let the materials speak, and keep color honest, because people should recognize the thing they ordered when it shows up at their door.

Whether I'm on a mountain or in the studio, the process doesn't change: slow down, notice what's already beautiful, and give the light time to do the rest.

Mia Navarro
Photographer and product designer
Silver Lake, Los Angeles

Book Club Reading List

Members: Lena, Priya, Vicki, and Mia. We meet once a month, usually at Lena's, and Vicki joins on FaceTime from San Francisco. Whoever hosts handles snacks. Whoever picked the book leads the conversation.

Now reading
- The Salt Orchard by Marisol Vega. Three generations of a family and their lemon groves on a Sicilian hillside. Lena's pick.

Up next
- Small Hours on Calle Luna by Tomás Avila. Won the group chat vote over Every Window Facing West.

Still on the list
- Every Window Facing West by Adele Strand. Runner-up, so it goes first next time.
- North of Quiet by June Hollander. Lena's nominee.
- The Glass Coast by Ines Marchetti. Priya's nominee.
- A Field Guide to Leaving by Wren Castellanos. Mia's nominee.

Already read
- The Lantern Year by Hollis Prewitt. Four stars.
- Everything Under the Fig Tree by Ana Ferreira-Doyle. Five stars, and everyone cried.
- Tidewater Hours by Callum Ashby. Three stars. Great ending, slow middle.

Ground rules
- Finish the book or don't, but come anyway.
- No spoilers in the group chat before we meet.
- Bring one passage you loved and read it out loud.
- The Eastside Book Fair is coming up, so let's go together and each bring back one book for the next round of nominations.

documents.title: Feld Ceramics — Brand Notes for Photographers
documents.body:
Feld Ceramics: Brand Notes for Photographers

Thank you for working with us! These notes keep our images consistent across the web shop, social, and the wholesale lookbook.

Who we are

Feld Ceramics is a two-person studio in Los Angeles making small-batch stoneware for everyday use. Every piece is thrown, trimmed, and glazed by hand, so no two are exactly alike. We want photos that feel calm, warm, and lived-in.

The new collection
- Sea Salt: matte white with soft blue flecks.
- Fig: deep purple-brown with drips that break to amber at the rim.
- Ash: speckled gray with a dry, stony texture.

Color and light
- Natural-looking light and soft shadows. Nothing glossy or overly bright.
- Backgrounds in warm gray, oat linen, or pale wood.
- Glaze color must be accurate. Customers order by color, and returns hurt a small studio.

Styling
- Real food and drinks are welcome: coffee, citrus, bread, fresh herbs.
- Keep props minimal, with no branded items or logos.
- Show scale with hands when it helps.

Please avoid
- Heavy filters or film presets.
- Hiding the maker's mark completely. We love a foot-ring detail shot.
- Stacking pieces that aren't designed to stack.

Deliverables
- 25 to 30 final images, full resolution, plus web crops at 1:1 and 4:5.
- A handful of behind-the-scenes shots for social, if there's time.

Questions on the day: Nora Feld, (323) 555-0112.

documents.title: Focaccia with Olives
documents.body:
Focaccia with Olives

Makes one 9×13 pan. Serves 8, or 4 if Dad is at the table.

Ingredients
- 500 g bread flour
- 400 g warm water
- 1 packet (7 g) instant yeast
- 12 g fine sea salt
- 1 tsp honey
- 6 tbsp extra virgin olive oil, divided
- 1 cup Castelvetrano and Kalamata olives, pitted and halved
- 2 sprigs fresh rosemary
- Zest of 1 lemon
- Flaky sea salt for the top

Method
- Whisk the water, honey, and yeast in a large bowl. Add the flour and salt and stir until no dry bits remain. The dough will be sticky and shaggy, and that's right.
- Drizzle 2 tablespoons of oil over the dough, cover, and refrigerate overnight, 12 to 24 hours.
- Pour 2 tablespoons of oil into the pan. Tip the dough in, fold the edges underneath, and let it rise at room temperature for 2 to 3 hours, until puffy and jiggly.
- Heat the oven to 450°F. Oil your fingers and press deep dimples all the way to the bottom of the pan.
- Scatter the olives and rosemary, pressing them in gently. Drizzle with the last of the oil and finish with flaky salt.
- Bake 25 to 30 minutes, until deep golden brown.
- Zest the lemon over the top straight out of the oven, then cool on a rack for 10 minutes so the bottom stays crisp.

Tip: Bake it the morning you're serving it. It's best within a few hours, and leftovers make great toast.
